title: Not Our Odyssey: Great Hearts Alumni on Nolan's Film
author: Caleb Gottry and Miguel Thompson
summary: Two Great Hearts classical-school alumni who studied and translated Homer's Odyssey in their Humane Letters and Greek coursework review Christopher Nolan's 70mm IMAX adaptation against the original poem, arguing Nolan's version is systematically sanitized and modernized in ways that reveal his own thematic preoccupations more than Homer's. Their central contrast is between Homer's hubris-driven, infallible Odysseus, whom gods and readers cheer for despite pillaging and lying his way home, and Nolan's trauma-broken, PTSD-inflected Odysseus who is ultimately exiled and made to seek repentance, a concept the authors note has no equivalent in the original poem. They trace this shift through specific textual choices: the removal of Odysseus's willing infidelity with Circe and Calypso, the diminishment of the Greek pantheon into a largely non-verbal Athena, and a new theme of radical hospitality toward the stranger that has no ancient precedent. While crediting Nolan's visual and musical fidelity, including instruments recreated to be historically authentic, they fault the film's dialogue for falling into modern slang rather than matching the poem's poetic register. The review closes by treating the film not as a replacement for Homer but as an introduction that should send viewers back to the actual text.
points: Locates the film's central departure precisely: Homer's Odyssey is a hubris narrative that never asks its hero to repent, while Nolan's version introduces repentance as an organizing theme that has no equivalent in the ancient poem.

Identifies the removal of Odysseus's willing infidelity with Circe and Calypso as a specific textual excision, attributing it to modern sensibilities about marriage that would complicate the redemption arc Nolan wants to tell.

Traces the diminishment of Homer's active, speaking pantheon into a largely non-verbal Athena-vision as a deliberate Nolan directorial pattern consistent with his treatment of the supernatural in the Dark Knight trilogy, while conceding it produces a more relatable modern narrative.

Distinguishes production fidelity (visuals, score, use of recreated ancient Greek instruments) from dialogue fidelity, arguing the film succeeds visually and musically but fails poetically by lapsing into modern slang.

Uses direct citation of Fagles's translation (violent and sexual passages) to demonstrate concretely how much rawer the source poem is than its R-rated film adaptation, grounding the 'sanitized' claim in textual evidence rather than assertion.
quotes: To put it succinctly, Homer's Odyssey is highly sexual, graphically violent and entirely pagan. It tells the story of an Odysseus bent by his hubris. Nolan's Odyssey is rarely sexual, tamely violent and largely areligious.
While most language learners start with may I use the restroom, please, ancient Greek scholars start with he knocked them dead like pups, their brains gushed out all over, soaked the floor
Homer, on the other hand, boasts a Herculean hero with destruction in his wake. But, as long as he gets home, the readers and the gods mourn with him and cheer for him.

The Odyssey, as Nolan has reimagined it, is a story of repentance, which is a concept that was not in the original poem. Homer's Greek heroes mourned the length of the Trojan war but certainly did not regret their bloody victory

This theme of radical hospitality further diminishes Odysseus's infallibility from the original poem, as he is forced into exile upon the murder of the suitors in the film rather than retaking his throne as he does in the poem.

Nolan's visuals and score are beautiful and true-to-text. The music is even composed using recreations of ancient Grecian instruments. One of our main issues following our viewing was not in the production value, but the dialogue
Nolan's Odyssey is no replacement for Homer's epic, but it is an introduction to the man of twists and turns through the lens of our not-so-ancient civilization and struggles.
